title: Does Leukemia Show Up in Blood Work? What a Leukemia Blood Test Can and Cannot Show
summary: Does leukemia show up in blood work? What a CBC shows in acute and chronic leukemia, why counts can mislead, how leukemia is diagnosed, and when to get care the same day.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


Leukemia often does show up on routine blood work. It is a cancer of the cells that make blood, so it usually changes the complete blood count (CBC), and the CBC is usually the first test that points to it. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) are often found on blood tests done for another reason, before any symptoms \[[1](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/cll-treatment-pdq) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000570.htm) \]. A CBC cannot diagnose leukemia, though. Abnormal counts have far more common causes, and leukemia is confirmed with a blood smear, flow cytometry and, for most types, a bone marrow test \[[3](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]. A normal or low[white blood cell count](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/white-blood-cell-count) also does not rule out acute leukemia: the white count is normal or low in about half of people with acute lymphoblastic leukemia and 40% of people with acute myeloid leukemia when they are diagnosed \[[4](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/multimedia/table/findings-at-diagnosis-in-the-most-common-leukemias) \].


This page covers one question: what blood work can and cannot show about leukemia, and what to do if you are worried or holding an abnormal result. For the symptoms themselves, see[early signs and symptoms of leukemia in adults](https://mitohealth.com/blog/early-signs-and-symptoms-of-leukemia-in-adults) . For lymphoma, which often leaves the blood count normal, see[does lymphoma show up in blood work](https://mitohealth.com/blog/does-lymphoma-show-up-in-blood-work) .


## The short answer


- **Blood work is usually where leukemia first shows.** The American Society of Hematology says a CBC can reveal leukemic cells, and that abnormal white cell levels or low red cell or platelet counts can suggest leukemia \[[5](https://www.hematology.org/education/patients/blood-cancers/leukemia) \].
- **Chronic leukemias are often found by chance.** The National Cancer Institute says CLL may cause no symptoms at first and be found during a routine blood test \[[1](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/cll-treatment-pdq) \]. MedlinePlus says most people with CML are diagnosed in its early phase, when they have blood tests for other reasons \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000570.htm) \].
- **Abnormal counts are clues, not a diagnosis.** MedlinePlus says a CBC is only one tool, and a low white count, for example, can come from an autoimmune disorder, a bone marrow disorder or cancer \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \]. A blood smear alone cannot diagnose a disease either \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/blood-smear/) \].
- **A normal count is reassuring, not proof.** Most people with acute leukemia have at least one clearly abnormal count at diagnosis \[[4](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/multimedia/table/findings-at-diagnosis-in-the-most-common-leukemias) \]. A single normal CBC still does not rule out leukemia that is just starting, so new or persistent symptoms deserve a new blood count.


## What a CBC can show in leukemia


A CBC counts red cells, white cells and platelets and measures hemoglobin \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \]. The version with a differential also counts each type of white cell, including lymphocytes and neutrophils. When the CBC is abnormal, a blood smear, also called a[peripheral blood film](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/peripheral-blood-film) , is often the next step: cells are spread on a slide and checked under a microscope to confirm the counts and look at the cells themselves \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/blood-smear/) \].


Leukemia changes the count in different ways depending on the type. The American Society of Hematology groups leukemias as acute or chronic: chronic forms progress more slowly, while acute forms need treatment right away \[[5](https://www.hematology.org/education/patients/blood-cancers/leukemia) \]. This table summarizes typical findings at diagnosis from the Merck Manual Professional Edition \[[4](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/multimedia/table/findings-at-diagnosis-in-the-most-common-leukemias) \]:


Type White cell count at diagnosis Red cells and platelets What the smear usually shows


Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) High in about 50%, normal or low in about 50% Severe anemia in more than 90%, low platelets in more than 80% Many lymphoblasts


Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) High in about 60%, normal or low in about 40% Severe anemia in more than 90%, low platelets in more than 90% Many myeloblasts


Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) High in about 98% Mild anemia in about 50%, low platelets in 20% to 30% Many small lymphocytes


Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) High in essentially all Mild anemia in about 80%, platelets high in about 60% The whole myeloid series


### Acute leukemia: blasts, anemia and low platelets


In acute leukemia, immature cells called blasts build up in the bone marrow and crowd out normal blood production. The American Cancer Society says most people with AML or ALL have too many immature white cells in their blood and not enough red cells or platelets \[[3](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]\[[8](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-lymphocytic-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]. Blasts are not normally found in the blood, so blasts on a smear are a finding that needs follow-up \[[3](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]\[[8](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-lymphocytic-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]. The Merck Manual says low counts across all three cell lines together with blasts in the blood suggest acute leukemia \[[9](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology-and-oncology/leukemias/acute-myeloid-leukemia-aml) \].


The total white count is a poor guide on its own. It is high in only about half of people with acute leukemia and normal or low in the rest \[[4](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/multimedia/table/findings-at-diagnosis-in-the-most-common-leukemias) \]. What usually points to acute leukemia is the combination: low red cells, low platelets, few normal infection-fighting cells, and blasts on the smear.


### Chronic lymphocytic leukemia: a high lymphocyte count


The National Cancer Institute says CLL often causes no signs or symptoms at first and may be found during a routine blood test \[[1](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/cll-treatment-pdq) \]. Its main sign is a high lymphocyte count. The American Cancer Society says more than 5,000 lymphocytes per cubic millimeter strongly suggests CLL, though other tests are still needed \[[10](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]. On the smear, CLL cells often appear as smudge cells \[[10](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]\[[11](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470433/) \].


A high lymphocyte count is far more often caused by something else. The Merck Manual names viral infection, such as mononucleosis, as the most common cause \[[12](https://www.merckmanuals.com/home/blood-disorders/white-blood-cell-disorders/lymphocytic-leukocytosis) \]. See[causes of high lymphocytes](https://mitohealth.com/blog/high-lymphocytes-causes) . A small abnormal population of B cells that stays below the CLL threshold is called monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis, and the Merck Manual reports that about 1% to 2% of cases progress to CLL each year \[[13](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology-and-oncology/leukemias/chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia-cll) \].


### Chronic myeloid leukemia: a high white count with immature cells


MedlinePlus says the CBC in CML shows an increased number of white blood cells with many immature forms, and platelets may also be high \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000570.htm) \]. The Merck Manual says CML is most often suspected from an abnormal CBC obtained incidentally, with granulocyte counts usually below 50,000 per microliter in people without symptoms and from 200,000 to 1,000,000 per microliter in people with symptoms \[[14](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology-and-oncology/leukemias/chronic-myeloid-leukemia-cml) \]. The smear often shows immature granulocytes along with more basophils and eosinophils than usual, which helps tell CML apart from a reactive rise in white cells \[[14](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology-and-oncology/leukemias/chronic-myeloid-leukemia-cml) \].


## Blood results that can prompt a closer look


Each result below can appear in leukemia. Each is far more often explained by something common. What turns a result into a reason for a closer look is that it persists on a repeat test, keeps moving in one direction, has no other explanation, or comes with the symptoms described further down.


Result How it can relate to leukemia Far more common causes


Blasts on the smear Blasts are not normally in the blood and are the hallmark of acute leukemia \[[3](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]\[[8](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-lymphocytic-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \] Few. The Merck Manual notes that reactive white cell rises from infection never show high blast counts \[[9](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology-and-oncology/leukemias/acute-myeloid-leukemia-aml) \]. Always follow up


[High white count](https://mitohealth.com/blog/everything-you-need-to-know-about-high-white-blood-cell-count) Typical of CML and CLL, and of about half of acute leukemias \[[4](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/multimedia/table/findings-at-diagnosis-in-the-most-common-leukemias) \] Infections, inflammatory disorders, allergic reactions and some steroids \[[15](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/blood-differential/) \]. See[which WBC levels are dangerous](https://mitohealth.com/guide/dangerous-wbc-thresholds)


[High lymphocytes](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/lymphocytes) The main sign of CLL \[[10](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \] Viral infections such as mononucleosis, and some bacterial infections \[[12](https://www.merckmanuals.com/home/blood-disorders/white-blood-cell-disorders/lymphocytic-leukocytosis) \]. See[causes of high lymphocytes](https://mitohealth.com/blog/high-lymphocytes-causes)


[Low white count](https://mitohealth.com/blog/low-white-blood-cell-count-what-does-it-mean) A shortage of normal infection-fighting cells is common in AML \[[16](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-symptoms.html) \] Certain medicines such as antibiotics, chemotherapy, HIV and other bone marrow diseases \[[15](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/blood-differential/) \]


[Low hemoglobin](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/hemoglobin) (anemia) Present in most acute leukemias at diagnosis \[[4](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/multimedia/table/findings-at-diagnosis-in-the-most-common-leukemias) \] Many non-cancer causes. See[is low hemoglobin a sign of cancer?](https://mitohealth.com/blog/is-low-hemoglobin-a-sign-of-cancer)


[Low platelets](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/platelet-count) Present in most acute leukemias at diagnosis \[[4](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/multimedia/table/findings-at-diagnosis-in-the-most-common-leukemias) \] Viral infections such as mononucleosis or hepatitis, autoimmune disease, cirrhosis and vitamin B12 deficiency \[[17](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/platelet-tests/) \]


Low counts in all three lines (pancytopenia) Together with blasts, suggests acute leukemia \[[9](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology-and-oncology/leukemias/acute-myeloid-leukemia-aml) \] The Merck Manual lists aplastic anemia, viral infections such as mononucleosis, and vitamin B12 or folate deficiency as causes to consider \[[9](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology-and-oncology/leukemias/acute-myeloid-leukemia-aml) \]


A very high white count deserves particular care. The American Cancer Society says that if the blast count gets very high, the cells can clog small blood vessels, a rare emergency called leukostasis \[[16](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-symptoms.html) \]. In someone without an obvious infection, a count far above the normal range is a reason to talk to a clinician the same day.


## Can you have leukemia with a normal CBC?


It is uncommon at the time of diagnosis, but a single normal CBC does not fully rule leukemia out.


The Merck Manual figures show why a completely normal CBC is unusual in leukemia that is already causing illness. Severe anemia is present in more than 90% of people with acute leukemia at diagnosis, and low platelets in more than 80% \[[4](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/multimedia/table/findings-at-diagnosis-in-the-most-common-leukemias) \]. A white count in the normal range, on the other hand, is common in acute leukemia, so a normal white count alone tells you little \[[4](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/multimedia/table/findings-at-diagnosis-in-the-most-common-leukemias) \].


There are three practical reasons a normal result does not settle the question:


- **Timing.** Acute leukemias progress quickly \[[5](https://www.hematology.org/education/patients/blood-cancers/leukemia) \]. A CBC done months ago, before symptoms began, says little about how the blood looks now. When symptoms are new or getting worse, the useful test is a new CBC.
- **Early chronic disease.** CLL is suspected once lymphocytes pass about 5,000 per cubic millimeter \[[10](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]. A small abnormal population of B cells below that level is classed as monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis rather than leukemia, and only a small share of cases go on to CLL \[[13](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology-and-oncology/leukemias/chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia-cll) \].
- **A single number misses the pattern.** A result that is in range but has moved steadily since your last test can matter more than one flagged value. Comparing results over time is what shows that movement.


The reverse holds too. Most abnormal CBCs are not leukemia. A high white count has many common causes, including infections, inflammatory disorders, allergic reactions and some steroids \[[15](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/blood-differential/) \]. MedlinePlus puts it simply: a CBC is only one tool, read alongside your history and symptoms \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \].


## What actually diagnoses leukemia


Blood counts raise the question. These tests answer it.


- **Peripheral blood smear.** The cells are examined under a microscope for blasts, smudge cells or immature forms. It can confirm what the CBC suggests, but MedlinePlus says a blood smear alone cannot diagnose a disease \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/blood-smear/) \].
- **Flow cytometry (immunophenotyping).** This test uses antibodies to read the proteins on the surface of cells and sort them by type \[[3](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]\[[18](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/adult-aml-treatment-pdq) \]. In CLL, flow cytometry on a blood sample is the key test. The American Cancer Society says bone marrow is tested only if blood tests or a lymph node biopsy do not give enough information, and the Merck Manual says a bone marrow biopsy is not required to diagnose CLL \[[10](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]\[[13](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology-and-oncology/leukemias/chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia-cll) \].
- **Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy.** A needle removes liquid marrow and a small piece of bone \[[3](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]. The American Cancer Society says acute leukemia usually is not diagnosed without looking at bone marrow cells \[[3](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]\[[8](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-lymphocytic-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]. AML generally requires at least 20% blasts in the marrow or blood, or at least 10% when certain gene or chromosome changes are present \[[3](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]. ALL generally requires blasts to make up at least 20% of marrow cells \[[8](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-lymphocytic-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \].
- **Genetic and chromosome tests.** Cytogenetics, FISH and molecular tests look for specific changes in the leukemia cells \[[18](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/adult-aml-treatment-pdq) \]\[[19](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/cml-treatment-pdq) \]. CML is diagnosed when tests find the BCR::ABL1 gene or the Philadelphia chromosome \[[20](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/chronic-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]. AML cells are often tested for changes in genes such as FLT3, IDH1, IDH2 and NPM1 \[[3](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \].


## Symptoms that matter alongside the blood count


The National Cancer Institute lists these signs of acute leukemia: weakness or feeling tired, fever, infections, pale skin, and easy bruising or bleeding. It notes that early symptoms may feel like the flu \[[18](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/adult-aml-treatment-pdq) \]\[[21](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/adult-all-treatment-pdq) \]. Chronic leukemias often cause no symptoms at first. When they do, the National Cancer Institute lists painless swollen lymph nodes, tiredness, fever, infections and drenching night sweats for CLL \[[1](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/cll-treatment-pdq) \], and weight loss, tiredness, night sweats, fever and pain or fullness below the left ribs for CML \[[19](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/cml-treatment-pdq) \].


Each of these has many everyday causes. For a fuller guide, see[early signs and symptoms of leukemia in adults](https://mitohealth.com/blog/early-signs-and-symptoms-of-leukemia-in-adults) .


### Patterns worth a visit


None of these means you have leukemia. Each is a reason to see a clinician and get a CBC rather than wait.


- **Tiredness, paleness or breathlessness that does not improve** , especially with easy bruising, frequent infections or fevers \[[16](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-symptoms.html) \]\[[22](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000542.htm) \].
- **New easy bruising, small red or purple spots on the skin, nosebleeds or bleeding gums** \[[16](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-symptoms.html) \]\[[22](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000542.htm) \].
- **An abnormal CBC that stays abnormal on a repeat test** , keeps moving in one direction, or shows more than one cell line out of range.
- **A high lymphocyte count that does not settle** weeks after an infection, especially with swollen lymph nodes or night sweats \[[1](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/cll-treatment-pdq) \].
- **Fullness or pain below the left ribs** from an enlarged spleen \[[19](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/cml-treatment-pdq) \].


### Same-day red flags


Get care the same day, or emergency care, for any of these:


- **Bleeding that will not stop** , such as a nosebleed that will not stop or a cut that keeps oozing. The American Cancer Society notes that acute promyelocytic leukemia, a type of AML, can cause problems with bleeding and blood clotting \[[16](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-symptoms.html) \].
- **Fever with a known low white count** , or a fever that will not go away \[[16](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-symptoms.html) \]\[[22](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000542.htm) \].
- **Stroke-like symptoms with a very high white count** : headache, weakness on one side, slurred speech, confusion, sleepiness, blurred vision or shortness of breath. These can be signs of leukostasis, which the American Cancer Society calls a medical emergency \[[16](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-symptoms.html) \].
- **A lab report that mentions blasts.** Blasts are not normally found in the blood \[[3](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/acute-myeloid-leukemia/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \], and acute leukemia needs treatment right away \[[5](https://www.hematology.org/education/patients/blood-cancers/leukemia) \]. Call the clinician who ordered the test that day.


## Which tests to bring to a clinician


If you are worried, a clinician will start with your history, an exam of your lymph nodes, liver and spleen, and a CBC. If a CBC is already done, bring the full report, including the differential and any comment about the smear, along with earlier results for comparison. A change over time often says more than a single value.


Test What it adds


[CBC with differential and platelets](https://mitohealth.com/products/complete-blood-count-cbc-with-differential-and-platelet-count) Red cells, each type of white cell, and platelets. The starting point for any leukemia question


Earlier CBC results Shows whether a value is new, stable or moving


[Comprehensive metabolic panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/comprehensive-metabolic-panel-cmp) Kidney and liver function, part of a standard CLL workup \[[1](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/cll-treatment-pdq) \]


[LDH](https://mitohealth.com/products/lactate-dehydrogenase-ldh) A marker of cell turnover that can be raised in CLL \[[1](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/cll-treatment-pdq) \]\[[13](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology-and-oncology/leukemias/chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia-cll) \]


[Uric acid](https://mitohealth.com/products/uric-acid-serum) Can be raised at diagnosis in CLL \[[13](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology-and-oncology/leukemias/chronic-lymphocytic-leukemia-cll) \]


None of these tests can confirm leukemia. The CBC is the useful starting point because it is the test most likely to show a change worth following, and it can show whether another cause, such as anemia or a recent infection, explains how you feel. The smear review, flow cytometry and any bone marrow test that follow are ordered by a clinician, usually a hematologist.


If the question is myeloma rather than leukemia, the useful blood tests are different. See[multiple myeloma blood tests](https://mitohealth.com/blog/multiple-myeloma-blood-test) .


Questions worth asking at the visit:


- Is anything in my CBC abnormal, and was a smear reviewed?
- Could an infection, a medicine or a nutrient deficiency explain this result?
- Should the CBC be repeated, and when?
- If it is still abnormal, do I need flow cytometry or a referral to a hematologist?

## Frequently asked questions


### Can a routine blood test detect leukemia?


Often, yes. Leukemia lives in the blood and bone marrow, so a complete blood count is usually abnormal and is often the first sign. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia and chronic myeloid leukemia are frequently found on blood tests done for another reason. A blood count cannot confirm leukemia, though. That takes a blood smear, flow cytometry and, for most types, a bone marrow test.


### What does a CBC look like with leukemia?


It depends on the type. Acute leukemias usually show anemia and low platelets, and the white count can be high, normal or low, often with immature cells called blasts. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia usually shows a high lymphocyte count. Chronic myeloid leukemia usually shows a high white count with immature cells, and platelets may be high.


### Can you have leukemia with a normal CBC?


It is uncommon at the time of diagnosis, but one normal count does not fully rule it out. Most people with acute leukemia have at least one clearly abnormal count when they are diagnosed. Acute leukemia progresses quickly, so a normal CBC from months ago says little about new symptoms. New or persistent symptoms deserve a new blood count.


### What white blood cell count indicates leukemia?


No single number does. In acute leukemia the white count is high in only about half of people, and normal or low in the rest. A lymphocyte count above 5,000 per microliter raises the question of chronic lymphocytic leukemia, but flow cytometry is needed to confirm it. High white counts have many more common causes, including infection, inflammation, allergic reactions and some steroids.


### What blood tests confirm leukemia?


A peripheral blood smear and flow cytometry are the main blood tests. Flow cytometry on blood is usually enough to diagnose chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Acute leukemia is usually confirmed by a bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, and chronic myeloid leukemia by finding the BCR::ABL1 gene or the Philadelphia chromosome. Genetic tests on the leukemia cells help classify the type.


### Should I worry about a high white blood cell count?


Usually not by itself. A high count has many common causes, including infection, inflammation, allergic reactions, stress, smoking and some steroids. A count that stays high, keeps rising, shows immature cells on the smear, or comes with low red cells or platelets is worth taking to a clinician promptly.
